ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All procedures were approved by the University of Toronto Research Ethics Board.
A total of 78 participants were exposed to statistical regularities embedded within continuous streams of syllables, presented visually at a fixed rate of 4 Hz.

Throughout exposure, participants were asked to complete a color-categorization task that was not related to the statistical structures, but was essential for our measurement of ongoing attentional fluctuations (Decker, Dubois, et al., 2023; Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023).
table.formatted: Throughout exposure, participants were asked to complete a color-categorization task that was not related to the statistical structures, but was essential for our measurement of ongoing attentional fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Decker, Dubois, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023)</ref>.

table.text: Eighty-seven participants took part in the study (59 women; mean age = 19.43 years, SD = 1.66).
All provided written informed consent and were compensated with $40 CAD or course credit.
Participants completed three conditions (Control, Frequency, and TP) in a counterbalanced within-subjects design.
After exposure to each of the two structured conditions, participants completed a Familiarity Judgment task followed by a Syllable Sorting task (task order fixed).
Participants were informed that the stream "may or may not contain a rule," and no information about the presence or nature of a pattern was provided before the Syllable Sorting task.
In each condition, participants were exposed to four syllable streams (i.e., blocks), interrupted by self-paced breaks.

table.text: Thus, the main logic behind our manipulation is that, if participants were sensitive to the statistical structure of the streams, neural synchronization to the periodic statistical structure should emerge at 1 Hz in the structured streams, reflecting perceptual detection of statistical patterns, and not in the Control condition.

table.text: In each stream, 128 of the 960 syllables were colored instead of being black (i.e., in each block, 113 items appeared in red, and 15 appeared in blue), and participants were instructed to press one key (Z) when a red syllable appeared and another key (M) when a blue syllable appeared.

table.text: After exposure to each structured condition (Frequency, TP), participants completed a Familiarity Judgment Task, where they rated four-syllable strings (displayed simultaneously as a single unit; e.g., za-si-ro-bu) on a 4-point Likert scale based on whether they followed the same presentation order seen during the exposure phase.
Participants were not informed of the rule but were encouraged to make their best judgment.

Following the Familiarity Judgment Task for the structured conditions, participants were informed about the statistical rule used to arrange the syllables in the exposure stream and were asked to perform a Syllable Sorting Task.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The role of Attentional Fluctuations in the Detection and Recall of Statistical Regularities
table.research_questions:
Directional:
Question 1. Does the presence of statistical regularities influence sustained attention? Hypothesis 1. We hypothesize that regularities may draw participants’ attention, leading to differences in sustained attention metrics (i.e., the percentage of time spent in a poor attentional state) between the control group and the two experimental conditions (frequency vs. TP). Specifically, we hypothesize that participants would exhibit fewer attentional lapses when statistical regularities are present compared to the control condition, suggesting increased attention.
Question 2. Do fluctuations in sustained attention affect our ability to detect statistical regularities, as reflected by neural entrainment in the brain? Hypotheses 2. We will use correlational analyses to examine whether neural entrainment at the regularity frequency (1 Hz) is associated with participants' attentional state (i.e., the percentage of time spent in a poor attentional state). If attention is related to neural entrainment to statistical regularities, we expect a negative correlation between attentional lapse frequency and the strength of neural entrainment.
Question 3. How does sustained attention impact the storage of statistical regularities in memory? Hypothesis 3. If sustained attention influences the storage of statistical regularities in memory, we would expect a correlation between participants’ accuracy on the Familiarity and/or Syllable Sorting Task and the sustained attention metric. The direction of this correlation is uncertain: if sustained attention facilitates the storage of regularities, a negative correlation between lapse rates and behavioral performance would be expected, meaning that as the percentage of time spent in a poor attentional state increases, task accuracy decreases. However, Decker, Dubois, Duncan, and Finn (2022) found that higher rates of attentional lapses correlated with greater learning of task-irrelevant information, suggesting that a positive correlation could indicate better memory storage of statistical regularities when more attentional lapses occur. If no correlation is found between the percentage of lapse rates and task accuracy, this would suggest that attention does not play a significant role in the explicit storage of statistical regularities, which will be discussed in the context of the limitations of null results.
Question 4. How do differences in the strength of neural entrainment for regularities impact the storage of statistical regularities in memory? Hypothesis 4. Prior research indicates that the strength of neural entrainment to statistical patterns correlates with implicit behavioral indicators of statistical learning (see Battering & Paller, 2017). This correlation suggests that, while neural and behavioral measures capture different aspects of learning, both reflect participants’ ability to internalize patterns. However, unpublished data from our lab suggest no correlation between neural entrainment and post-learning behavioral sensitivity to statistical regularities. The present study will therefore extend our knowledge to previously untested conditions. Should a positive correlation emerge, it would indicate that neural entrainment to statistical patterns not only reflects neural  pattern detection but also individual differences in memory storage and recall.
Exploratory:
Question 5 and 6. Are different types of statistical patterns processed differently in the brain? Is performance on behavioral statistical learning tasks influenced by the type of statistical patterns? Hypotheses 5 and 6. Statistical regularities based on transitional probabilities have been associated with participants' ability to store and recall patterns for later use (e.g., Saffran, Aslin, & Newport, 1996). However, to our best knowledge, there is no clear evidence that frequency-based groupings produce the same effect. Moreover, no study has directly investigated whether different statistical patterns (e.g., frequency vs. transitional probabilities) lead to differences in (1) neural entrainment or (2) participants' ability to recall regularities for post-exposure tasks. Given the limited evidence in literature, we cannot make clear predictions. However, if distinct types of statistical patterns are processed differently in the brain, we anticipate observable differences in the strength of neural entrainment and/or behavioral performance on the Familiarity Task between the frequency and TP conditions.
Question 7. Do more predictable items in the FPVS stream affect participants' performance and/or attentional state differently from less predictable items? Hypothesis 7. Transitional probabilities (TPs) enable the prediction of which item will appear next in the sequence. In our design, the first syllable of each non-existent word will be less predictable (TP = 0.33) compared to the following three syllables, which will have a high predictability (TP = 1). Given this contrast in predictability, we aim to investigate whether participants' attentional state or response times vary based on syllable position within the word. If predictability plays a role in modulating attention, we expect to observe differences in attentional lapse metrics and/or response times between the first syllable (less predictable) and the subsequent syllables (more predictable). We also consider the possibility of a graded effect, where attentional lapses/response times progressively change from the first to the last syllable within each word. Specifically, should a difference emerge, we hypothesize fewer attentional lapses/faster response times for predictable rather than unpredictable stimuli. In relation to frequency grouping (i.e., the statistical pattern presented in the frequency condition), base stimuli presented in the first three positions within each second are distinguished from the fourth syllable (oddball stimulus) based on their relative frequency during the stimulation. This frequency pattern is supposed to elicit differences at the level of groups of syllables and not an item-level, thus we do not expect to find significant differences in response times or attentional states between base and oddball syllables. However, if the oddball (deviant) stimuli impact participants’ performance, we might observe differences in the aforementioned measures between base and oddball stimuli.
Question 8. How does neural entrainment differ when participants are in versus out of the zone (in “good” versus “bad” attentional states)? Hypothesis 8. If neural entrainment is enhanced by attention, we hypothesize that it will be stronger when participants are in a good attentional state (i.e., for trials classified as “in-the-zone” compared to when they are in a bad attentional state (i.e., for trials classified as “out-of-the-zone”). If neural entrainment is not altered by attention, then it will be similar regardless of whether participants are in or out of the zone.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview: This experiment employs a within-subject design with three conditions: control, frequency, and TP conditions. In each condition, participants will complete a Sustained Attention Task. During the frequency and TP conditions, they will additionally perform two tasks: a Familiarity Task and a Syllable Sorting Task.
table.randomization: The order of condition presentation is counterbalanced for each participant. Stimuli are different across conditions (i.e., different groups of syllables are used in each condition) and counterbalanced across participants.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to accessing the data
table.existing_data_explanation:
A pilot study with 10 participants was conducted prior to this preregistration to explore the data and evaluate the validity of the paradigm and analysis methods. The pilot data will not be included in the final sample. Non-pilot data collection has started but analyses will not begin until this pre-registration is filed. 

None of the analyses outlined in this preregistration have been conducted on our data. All analyses were performed on a separate pilot sample, which did not inform the hypotheses presented here. The pilot data has only been accessed for quality control purposes. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether the modification to the Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation Paradigm still elicited the expected neural entrainment in the brain and whether the planned sustained attention analysis provided a valid measure of attentional processes for this specific paradigm.
table.data_collection_procedures:
To be enrolled in the experiment, participants must be fluent English speakers, between 18 and 35 years of age, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and with no record of neurological, or language impairment. All genders will be included in the study. In exchange for participation, participants will receive either a monetary reimbursement of 40$ (20$/h) or course credits. 
Exclusion Criteria 
Participants will be excluded from the analysis if their overall discrimination accuracy in the Sustained Attention Task is less than 75%. We reserve the right to adjust our exclusion criteria based on the final data (e.g., the distribution of the participants’ performance in the Sustained Attention Task turns out to be substantially better, or worse, than expected), but we will clearly justify and document any changes made.
table.sample_size: 78 participants who meet the inclusion criteria will be included in the study.
table.sample_size_rationale: For our power analysis, we focused on the primary research question that requires the highest statistical power: the individual-difference correlation between neural entrainment and behavioral data. Drawing on the only other study (Batterink and Paller, 2017) that examined the relationship between neural entrainment (using a different measure) and behavior (also with a different behavioral measure), we anticipate a small to moderate effect size, with a correlation around 0.33. Using the pwr toolbox in R, we determined that a minimum sample size of 65-75 participants is needed to achieve adequate power. To achieve a full counterbalanced sample, we set the final sample to 78 participants.
table.stopping_rule: We will conclude data collection once we have recruited 78 participants who meet the inclusion criteria for the study and do not fall under any of the exclusion criteria.
table.manipulated_variables:
Manipulated variables
Sustained Attention Task: To measure sustained attention, we manipulate the relative frequency of blue and red syllables in the experiment. Ninety percent of the trials feature red syllables (frequent trials), while 10% involve blue syllables (infrequent trials). Since black syllables are interspersed between these trials, it's important to note that, in this study, a "trial" refers to a colored syllable (i.e., red or blue syllables) requiring a participant's response.
To gather electrophysiological data on participants’ detection of regularities, we manipulate the presence of statistical patterns in the Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation (FPVS) stream. Specifically, we vary the arrangement of syllables to create either random sequences (control condition) or specific statistical regularities— frequency differences in the frequency condition and transitional probabilities in the TP condition.
Familiarity Task: We manipulated the structure of the syllable strings presented during the task. In the frequency condition, we varied the frequency of the oddball syllables within the string. The levels of correctness were: (1) correct—three base syllables and one oddball, (2) partially wrong—two base syllables and two oddballs, and (3) completely wrong—one base syllable and three oddballs. For the TP condition, we manipulated the structure of the non-word presented to participants. The levels of correctness were: (1) correct—a “word” presented during the FPVS stream, (2) partially wrong—the ending part of one “word” combined with the starting part of another, forming a high transitional probability incorrect string, and (3) completely wrong—a string composed of one syllable from each “word” presented during FPVS, resulting in a low transitional probability string.
Syllable Sorting Task: In this task, no variables are manipulated. Participants will simply be presented with a drag and drop task and asked to recreate the statistical structure that was presented during FPVS by sorting syllables in different boxes.

table.indices:
1. Mean classification accuracy • for frequent (red) and infrequent (blue) trials during the Sustained Attention Task for each participant.
Sustained attention analyses:
Building on previous research demonstrating that trial-by-trial fluctuations in RT deviance (Esterman et al., 2014) and speed (DeBettencourt et al., 2018) are linked to variations in attention and task performance, we aim to identify the most suitable index of sustained attention to use in our analyses. Following previous work (Decker, Dubois, Duncan & Finn, 2022) we adopted a data-driven approach to compare how well a moving average of RT speed versus RT deviance predicts trial-by-trial accuracy. Based on pilot data from 10 participants, RT speed appears to be a more sensitive indicator of attentional lapses than RT deviance (see Decker, Dubois, Duncan, Finn, 2022). Therefore, we plan to focus our primary analyses on RT speed and provide details on this index here, while reporting RT deviance results in the supplementary materials for completeness. However, we will verify whether RT speed remains the best predictor when analyzing data from the final sample. If RT speed is no longer the most sensitive indicator of attentional lapses, we will instead use RT deviance as our primary measure.
2. Response times  • For each participant, response times will be regressed onto trial number, and residuals will be extracted and used in all analyses. Subsequent references to response time refer to residualized response times. Residual response times will also be mean centered within participants, condition and block.
3. The mean absolute deviation of response time during the Sustained Attention task, for each trial for each participant. 
4. Smoothed variance time course
• First, residualized response times for missed and infrequent trials will be interpolated linearly by averaging response time data from the four surrounding trials (two trials before, two after). Since participants are allowed to take breaks between blocks, interpolation is done within each block and condition. In the case that observations from the four surrounding trials are missing, the window size is automatically increased until there are at least two non-missing values.
• Mean absolute RT deviance for each trial (the absolute value of the difference between a trial’s RT and a participant’s mean RT).
• Smoothed absolute RT deviance for each trial: mean absolute RT deviance values are smoothed using a three-trial moving average.
5.  Attentional zone
• A categorical variable indicating participants’ attentional state on each trial. 
• The median value of each participant’s smoothed variance time course data will be identified, and these values will be averaged across participants to produce a single value. 
• This single value will be used as a “cut-off” to assign participants’ response time data on each trial to either a low or high variability zone. Trials whose response time deviates more than this cut-off value will be coded as “poor”, whereas trials that deviate less will be coded as “good”. For analyses based on speed, trials will be coded as "poor" if the moving time course of RT speed exceeds the participant's mean moving time course and deviates more than the group threshold.
6.  Attentional zone percent • Based on the variable attention zone, we will calculate the percentage of total trials that each participant encodes during a good vs. poor attentional state. 

Familiarity Task:
7. Mean Ratings • we will calculate the mean ratings for each trial type (correct, partially wrong, completely wrong)

Sorting Task:
8. Sorting Accuracy (for frequency condition) •  Accuracy for each trial (i.e., for each of the 16 syllables) will be coded as 1 when oddballs are categorized as 'infrequent' and bases as 'frequent' in the Syllable Sorting Task.
9. Transitional Probability Accuracy (for the TP condition) • This measure assesses how accurately participants grouped syllables based on their transitional probability (TP), specifically focusing on adjacent syllables where TP = 1. The measure involves three checks: Same Box Check: Determines whether syllables from the same word are placed in the same box (as the aforementioned measure). Relative Position Check: Verifies that syllables in the same box maintain the correct relative order. Adjacency Check: Confirms that the syllables are adjacent in the expected sequence (TP = 1). A pair is marked as TRUE only if all three conditions are met, indicating correct placement based on TP. The final accuracy is calculated as the mean proportion of TRUE scores across all syllable pairs, providing a measure of how well participants grouped adjacent syllables according to their TP.
10. Position Accuracy (for the TP condition) • This measure evaluates the effect of syllable absolute position on participants' performance. It is calculated by comparing the expected position of each syllable with its observed position.
table.statistical_tests:
Question 1. Does the presence of statistical regularities influence sustained attention? We will use mixed-model analyses to assess the effect of condition on attentional lapses. We will run a mixed model analysis to predict attentional lapse scores across the three conditions Example code 1)  glmer(zone ~ condition + (1 | sbj), data = dataframe, family = binomial). Additional models will include predictors such as condition, condition order and trial order, possibly with their interactions as well: example code 2) glmer(zone ~ condition + condition_order +/* trial_order + (1 | sbj), data = dataframe, family = binomial). 
Question 2. Do fluctuations in sustained attention affect our ability to detect regularities, as reflected by neural entrainment in the brain? For each condition containing statistical regularities (i.e., Frequency and TP conditions), we will examine the correlation between neural entrainment at 1 Hz and attentional lapse scores within the same condition. If the assumptions of Pearson’s correlation are met, we will use this test to quantify the relationship.
Question 3. How does sustained attention impact the storage of statistical regularities in memory? 
We will examine the correlation between attentional lapse scores and the indices derived from the familiarity and syllable sorting tasks to assess whether attention influences participants’ ability to explicitly store and recall statistical regularities. If the assumptions of Pearson’s correlation are met, we will use this test; otherwise, we will apply a suitable non-parametric alternative. These correlations will be conducted separately for the TP and Frequency conditions.
Question 4. How do differences in the strength of neural entrainment for regularities impact the storage of statistical regularities in memory? We will compute Pearson correlations between participants' neural entrainment to statistical regularities and their accuracy indices from all behavioral tasks, provided that all assumptions are met. This analysis will be conducted separately for the TP and Frequency conditions.
Throughout the analyses, we will consider adding random slopes for subjects, to account for subject-specific variability in the overall, fixed effects. We will try them out and see whether the fitting process can sustain it (e.g., no singularity or convergence issues emerge).
table.inference_criteria: We will use p values (two-tailed). An effect will be considered significant if p < 0.05.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants will be excluded from the analysis if their overall discrimination accuracy in the Sustained Attention Task is less than 75%. Additionally, individual trial response times that are exceptionally fast or slow, and thus considered unreliable, will be excluded. As stated before, since cutoff values for response times will be determined based on the response time distribution across all participants, we will not specify them in advance. We reserve the right to adjust our data exclusion criteria based on the final data, but we will clearly justify and document any changes made.

Question 1. Does the presence of statistical regularities influence sustained attention? Hypothesis 1. We hypothesize that regularities may draw participants’ attention, leading to differences in sustained attention metrics (i.e., the percentage of time spent in a poor attentional state) between the control group and the two experimental conditions (frequency vs. TP). Specifically, we hypothesize that participants would exhibit fewer attentional lapses when statistical regularities are present compared to the control condition, suggesting increased attention.
Question 2. Do fluctuations in sustained attention affect our ability to detect statistical regularities, as reflected by neural entrainment in the brain? Hypotheses 2. We will use correlational analyses to examine whether neural entrainment at the regularity frequency (1 Hz) is associated with participants' attentional state (i.e., the percentage of time spent in a poor attentional state). If attention is related to neural entrainment to statistical regularities, we expect a negative correlation between attentional lapse frequency and the strength of neural entrainment.
Question 3. How does sustained attention impact the storage of statistical regularities in memory? Hypothesis 3. If sustained attention influences the storage of statistical regularities in memory, we would expect a correlation between participants’ accuracy on the Familiarity and/or Syllable Sorting Task and the sustained attention metric. The direction of this correlation is uncertain: if sustained attention facilitates the storage of regularities, a negative correlation between lapse rates and behavioral performance would be expected, meaning that as the percentage of time spent in a poor attentional state increases, task accuracy decreases. However, Decker, Dubois, Duncan, and Finn (2022) found that higher rates of attentional lapses correlated with greater learning of task-irrelevant information, suggesting that a positive correlation could indicate better memory storage of statistical regularities when more attentional lapses occur. If no correlation is found between the percentage of lapse rates and task accuracy, this would suggest that attention does not play a significant role in the explicit storage of statistical regularities, which will be discussed in the context of the limitations of null results.
Question 4. How do differences in the strength of neural entrainment for regularities impact the storage of statistical regularities in memory? Hypothesis 4. Prior research indicates that the strength of neural entrainment to statistical patterns correlates with implicit behavioral indicators of statistical learning (see Battering & Paller, 2017). This correlation suggests that, while neural and behavioral measures capture different aspects of learning, both reflect participants’ ability to internalize patterns. However, unpublished data from our lab suggest no correlation between neural entrainment and post-learning behavioral sensitivity to statistical regularities. The present study will therefore extend our knowledge to previously untested conditions. Should a positive correlation emerge, it would indicate that neural entrainment to statistical patterns not only reflects neural pattern detection but also individual differences in memory storage and recall.
Exploratory:
Question 5 and 6. Are different types of statistical patterns processed differently in the brain? Is performance on behavioral statistical learning tasks influenced by the type of statistical patterns? Hypotheses 5 and 6. Statistical regularities based on transitional probabilities have been associated with participants' ability to store and recall patterns for later use (e.g., Saffran, Aslin, & Newport, 1996). However, to our best knowledge, there is no clear evidence that frequency-based groupings produce the same effect. Moreover, no study has directly investigated whether different statistical patterns (e.g., frequency vs. transitional probabilities) lead to differences in (1) neural entrainment or (2) participants' ability to recall regularities for post-exposure tasks. Given the limited evidence in literature, we cannot make clear predictions. However, if distinct types of statistical patterns are processed differently in the brain, we anticipate observable differences in the strength of neural entrainment and/or behavioral performance on the Familiarity Task between the frequency and TP conditions.
Question 7. Do more predictable items in the FPVS stream affect participants' performance and/or attentional state differently from less predictable items? Hypothesis 7. Transitional probabilities (TPs) enable the prediction of which item will appear next in the sequence. In our design, the first syllable of each non-existent word will be less predictable (TP = 0.33) compared to the following three syllables, which will have a high predictability (TP = 1). Given this contrast in predictability, we aim to investigate whether participants' attentional state or response times vary based on syllable position within the word. If predictability plays a role in modulating attention, we expect to observe differences in attentional lapse metrics and/or response times between the first syllable (less predictable) and the subsequent syllables (more predictable). We also consider the possibility of a graded effect, where attentional lapses/response times progressively change from the first to the last syllable within each word. Specifically, should a difference emerge, we hypothesize fewer attentional lapses/faster response times for predictable rather than unpredictable stimuli. In relation to frequency grouping (i.e., the statistical pattern presented in the frequency condition), base stimuli presented in the first three positions within each second are distinguished from the fourth syllable (oddball stimulus) based on their relative frequency during the stimulation. This frequency pattern is supposed to elicit differences at the level of groups of syllables and not an item-level, thus we do not expect to find significant differences in response times or attentional states between base and oddball syllables. However, if the oddball (deviant) stimuli impact participants’ performance, we might observe differences in the aforementioned measures between base and oddball stimuli.
Question 8. How does neural entrainment differ when participants are in versus out of the zone (in “good” versus “bad” attentional states)? Hypothesis 8. If neural entrainment is enhanced by attention, we hypothesize that it will be stronger when participants are in a good attentional state (i.e., for trials classified as “in-the-zone” compared to when they are in a bad attentional state (i.e., for trials classified as “out-of-the-zone”). For the contrast between correct and completely wrong items, the linear model revealed no main effect of structure-rate neural entrainment, F (1, 152) = 1.34, p = .249, and no main effect of condition, F (1, 152) = 0.006, p = .940.
The interaction between structure-rate neural entrainment and condition was significant, F (1, 152) = 4.72, p = .031.

Considering the contrast between correct and partially wrong strings, the model revealed a significant effect of structure-rate neural entrainment, F (1, 152) = 6.57, p = .011, no main effect of condition, F (1, 152) = 0.12, p = .725, and no significant interaction between neural entrainment and condition, F (1, 152) = 0.001, p = .895.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps > .05", Text = "As expected, the Control condition showed no evidence of entrainment at this frequency (both ps > .05), whereas both structured conditions (Frequency and TP) showed reliable entrainment (all ps < .001; see Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 9 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: In line with our predictions, higher lapse rates were associated with lower accuracy (b = -0.05, SE = 0.02, t = -3.02, p = .003).
Relative to the Control condition, entrainment was stronger in both the Frequency (b = 0.04, SE = 0.005, t = 7.13, p < .001) and the TP condition (b = 0.07, SE = 0.005, t = 14.13, p < .001).
Relative to the Control condition, entrainment was stronger in both the Frequency (b = 0.04, SE = 0.005, t = 7.13, p < .001) and the TP condition (b = 0.07, SE = 0.005, t = 14.13, p < .001).
Neural entrainment was also significantly stronger in the TP condition than in the Frequency condition (b = 0.04, SE = 0.005, t = 7.00, p < .001).

Consistent with this weak overall effect, ratings did not differ reliably between correct and entirely wrong strings (b = 0.05, SE = 0.03, t = 1.72, p = .199), nor between correct and partially wrong strings (b = -0.01, SE = 0.03, t = -0.41, p = .910).

Consistent with this weak overall effect, ratings did not differ reliably between correct and entirely wrong strings (b = 0.05, SE = 0.03, t = 1.72, p = .199), nor between correct and partially wrong strings (b = -0.01, SE = 0.03, t = -0.41, p = .910).

However, sorting accuracy (M = 0.55, SD = 0.15; Fig. 3b) was significantly above chance (0.50), t = 2.59, p = .011, d = 0.29, 95% CI [0.51, 0.58], indicating reliable discrimination of frequency-based structure beyond initial exposure on one of two measures.
Post-hoc comparisons revealed that ratings were higher for correct than completely wrong strings (b = 0.07, SE = 0.03, t = 2.35, p = .049).

By contrast, ratings for partially wrong strings did not differ from correct items (b = 0.05, SE = 0.03, t = 1.53, p = .275), suggesting that participants did not reliably distinguish between fully and partially structured strings.

Sorting accuracy (M = 0.09, SD = 0.10; Fig. 3b) was above chance (0.05), t = 3.63, p < .001, d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.07, 0.11], further indicating that participants gained at least some explicit knowledge of the TP structure.

For the contrast between correct and completely wrong items, the linear model revealed no main effect of structure-rate neural entrainment, F (1, 152) = 1.34, p = .249, and no main effect of condition, F (1, 152) = 0.006, p = .940.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 66 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified
1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "eeg_data.txt", Column = "V6", Issues = "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 2808 values are missing"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: All procedures were approved by the University of Toronto Research Ethics Board.
live_data_statements: A total of 78 participants were exposed to statistical regularities embedded within continuous streams of syllables, presented visually at a fixed rate of 4 Hz.

Throughout exposure, participants were asked to complete a color-categorization task that was not related to the statistical structures, but was essential for our measurement of ongoing attentional fluctuations (Decker, Dubois, et al., 2023; Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023).
Eighty-seven participants took part in the study (59 women; mean age = 19.43 years, SD = 1.66).
All provided written informed consent and were compensated with $40 CAD or course credit.
Participants completed three conditions (Control, Frequency, and TP) in a counterbalanced within-subjects design.
After exposure to each of the two structured conditions, participants completed a Familiarity Judgment task followed by a Syllable Sorting task (task order fixed).
Participants were informed that the stream "may or may not contain a rule," and no information about the presence or nature of a pattern was provided before the Syllable Sorting task.
In each condition, participants were exposed to four syllable streams (i.e., blocks), interrupted by self-paced breaks.

Thus, the main logic behind our manipulation is that, if participants were sensitive to the statistical structure of the streams, neural synchronization to the periodic statistical structure should emerge at 1 Hz in the structured streams, reflecting perceptual detection of statistical patterns, and not in the Control condition.

In each stream, 128 of the 960 syllables were colored instead of being black (i.e., in each block, 113 items appeared in red, and 15 appeared in blue), and participants were instructed to press one key (Z) when a red syllable appeared and another key (M) when a blue syllable appeared.

After exposure to each structured condition (Frequency, TP), participants completed a Familiarity Judgment Task, where they rated four-syllable strings (displayed simultaneously as a single unit; e.g., za-si-ro-bu) on a 4-point Likert scale based on whether they followed the same presentation order seen during the exposure phase.
Participants were not informed of the rule but were encouraged to make their best judgment.

Following the Familiarity Judgment Task for the structured conditions, participants were informed about the statistical rule used to arrange the syllables in the exposure stream and were asked to perform a Syllable Sorting Task.

In the Frequency condition, 1 Hz 1 2 time (s) za si ro bu pa ku vi fu ci za za pa bu ci ku ku lo si ci ci ro pa bu bu jo ku ha TP Frequency Control a Trial Number Smoothed RT Deviance (ms) 0 50 100 0 100 50 150 b za �si bu pa ku Press Z Press M Press Z �ro out-zone in-zone participants were presented with all 16 syllables from the exposure stream in a random arrangement at the center of the screen.
For both tasks, participants were given unlimited time but were required to sort every syllable before moving forward with the experiment.
Participants were individually tested in a dimly lit room and positioned in front of a ZOWIE XL LCD Windows monitor with a screen resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels, and a 60 Hz refresh rate.

To measure individual differences in sustained attention, we computed lapse rates as the proportion of trials in which participants were in a poor attentional state (i.e., out-of-zone), following previous work (Debettencourt et al., 2018; Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023; Esterman et al., 2013; Fortenbaugh et al., 2018).
We investigated whether participants were able to group syllables solely on the basis of their absolute position within a sequence.

#### Reported vs. reproduced
68 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 22 matched (21 fully, 1 partially) — 32.4% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.
#### MATLAB code, no reproducible output

67 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. text.text: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them.
Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states?

To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment-the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities-alongside fluctuations in attentional states.
Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states.
Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses.
Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment.
Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses.
And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus.

Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.
Humans have a formidable capacity to learn from statistical regularities in the environment.

This capacity-commonly referred to as statistical learning-has been proposed as a mechanism underlying a wealth of fundamental cognitive skills, including visual learning (Fiser & Aslin, 2001), word identification (Lelonkiewicz et al., 2023; Saffran et al., 1996), semantic memory (Andrews et al., 2009), and even syntactic processing (Kidd, 2012).
text.formatted: This capacity-commonly referred to as statistical learning-has been proposed as a mechanism underlying a wealth of fundamental cognitive skills, including visual learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fiser & Aslin, 2001)</ref>, word identification <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lelonkiewicz et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Saffran et al., 1996)</ref>, semantic memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andrews et al., 2009)</ref>, and even syntactic processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kidd, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for statistical learning has been documented across development, from the cradle to the grave (Forest et al., 2023), and across species (Conway & Christiansen, 2001; Santolin & Saffran, 2018).
text.formatted: Evidence for statistical learning has been documented across development, from the cradle to the grave <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Forest et al., 2023)</ref>, and across species <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Conway & Christiansen, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Santolin & Saffran, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although various questions remain about how statistical learning interfaces with and even differs from other known cognitive processes (Frost et al., 2019), it is unquestionably a widespread learning mechanism, enabling the organization and interpretation of structured information in our environments (Sherman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Although various questions remain about how statistical learning interfaces with and even differs from other known cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Frost et al., 2019)</ref>, it is unquestionably a widespread learning mechanism, enabling the organization and interpretation of structured information in our environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Sherman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One pressing question about statistical learning concerns its relationship with attention.
Does attention constrain and shape this learning system, like it does for other forms of learning (Decker & Duncan, 2020)?
text.formatted: Does attention constrain and shape this learning system, like it does for other forms of learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Decker & Duncan, 2020</ref>)?

text.text: Or does statistical learning log environmental regularities regardless of our attentional goals and states?
Knowing the answer is critical for understanding how and when humans learn about the world around them.
On the one hand, statistical learning is often described as an implicit phenomenon, which can easily happen outside of attention (Batterink & Paller, 2019; Duncan & Theeuwes, 2020).
text.formatted: On the one hand, statistical learning is often described as an implicit phenomenon, which can easily happen outside of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Batterink & Paller, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Duncan & Theeuwes, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, numerous studies have reported that diverting attention away from structured input can impair statistical learning (Duncan et al., 2025; Toro et al., 2005; Turk-Browne et al., 2005).
text.formatted: On the other hand, numerous studies have reported that diverting attention away from structured input can impair statistical learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Duncan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Toro et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Turk-Browne et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These divergent findings likely reflect methodological factors.

Among them, in previous studies attention is manipulated exogenously-most often by perturbing attentional allocation through demanding concurrent tasks-without directly quantifying attentional engagement to the regularities, such that attention to the input may vary across studies and individuals.

Another important point is that this previous work often assesses statistical learning during a post-test after learning has already happened, often using tasks that require explicit judgments or strategic retrieval.

Such offline measures are likely to recruit aspects of cognition beyond online statistical learning processes (Batterink et al., 2015; Siegelman et al., 2018) and are subject to idiosyncratic task-strategy effects, cloaking the online dynamics of learning.
text.formatted: Such offline measures are likely to recruit aspects of cognition beyond online statistical learning processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Batterink et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Siegelman et al., 2018)</ref> and are subject to idiosyncratic task-strategy effects, cloaking the online dynamics of learning.

text.text: Most importantly, these approaches preclude direct examination of how naturally occurring fluctuations in sustained attention interact with the moment-by-moment processing of statistical structure.
Here, we address this fundamental gap in our knowledge by tracking statistical learning alongside the natural ups and downs of attention.

To this end, we leverage neural entrainment-the synchronization of neural activity to higher-order temporal structure in sensory input (Batterink & Paller, 2017)-as an online index of statistical learning.
text.formatted: To this end, we leverage neural entrainment-the synchronization of neural activity to higher-order temporal structure in sensory input <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Batterink & Paller, 2017)</ref>-as an online index of statistical learning.

text.text: Because attention naturally fluctuates over time, alternating between periods of focus and inattention (Debettencourt et al., 2018; Esterman et al., 2013; Fortenbaugh et al., 2018), this neural synchronization necessarily operates under dynamically varying attentional states.
text.formatted: Because attention naturally fluctuates over time, alternating between periods of focus and inattention <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Debettencourt et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Esterman et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fortenbaugh et al., 2018)</ref>, this neural synchronization necessarily operates under dynamically varying attentional states.

text.text: Importantly, neural entrainment to structure can be observed even when post-learning behavioral measures do not reflect learning (Farthouat et al., 2017; Ruzza & Crepaldi, 2026), and in populations with markedly reduced or absent conscious awareness, including sleeping neonates (Fló et al., 2022), sleeping adults (Batterink & Zhang, 2022), and minimally conscious patients (Benjamin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Importantly, neural entrainment to structure can be observed even when post-learning behavioral measures do not reflect learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Farthouat et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ruzza & Crepaldi, 2026)</ref>, and in populations with markedly reduced or absent conscious awareness, including sleeping neonates <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fló et al., 2022)</ref>, sleeping adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Batterink & Zhang, 2022)</ref>, and minimally conscious patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Benjamin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We do not yet know if neural entrainment simply persists in states of reduced attention, or is actively amplified when attention is fully engaged.

If entrainment and attention are related, it would show that our brains are not only passively responsive to the presence or absence of structure; rather, it would suggest that our brains interact with our internal cognitive states to enhance processing when we are "in the zone".
The current preregistered study was designed to reveal the interplay between neural sensitivity to structure and fluctuations in attentional focus.
A total of 78 participants were exposed to statistical regularities embedded within continuous streams of syllables, presented visually at a fixed rate of 4 Hz.

Across conditions, the visual input was closely matched but differed in statistical structure: streams either contained a regularity in which lower-frequency syllables appeared periodically at 1 Hz among higher-frequency syllables (Frequency condition); a regularity where syllables were grouped into fixed four-syllable units and also occurred at 1 Hz (Transitional Probability, TP, condition); or no statistical structure at all (Control condition).

Throughout exposure, participants were asked to complete a color-categorization task that was not related to the statistical structures, but was essential for our measurement of ongoing attentional fluctuations (Decker, Dubois, et al., 2023; Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023).
text.formatted: Throughout exposure, participants were asked to complete a color-categorization task that was not related to the statistical structures, but was essential for our measurement of ongoing attentional fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Decker, Dubois, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we assessed learning through post-exposure behavioral tasks, which allowed us to evaluate whether neural sensitivity to statistical structure during exposure translated into subsequent behavioral evidence of learning.
We tested whether endogenous fluctuations in sustained attention can predict the degree of neural entrainment to statistical regularities.

If attention constrains the real-time perception of statistical regularities, then attentional lapses-indexed by increased response time (RT) variability and classified as periods spent out-of-zone-should be associated with reduced neural entrainment to regularities.
Alternatively, if neural entrainment reflects processes that are independent of sustained attention, entrainment may be preserved during periods of reduced attentional engagement.
To preview, we found a strong relationship between attentional lapses and entrainment, both across and within individuals.

These findings show that trial-by-trial fluctuations in attention covary with neural sensitivity to statistical structure during online exposure, indicating that neural entrainment appears to reflect an attention-sensitive index of learning.
Eighty-seven participants took part in the study (59 women; mean age = 19.43 years, SD = 1.66).

Per preregistered criteria (18-35 years old, right-handed, fluent English speakers with normal or corrected vision and no cognitive, linguistic, or neurological conditions), nine were excluded (two for < 75% accuracy, two left-handed, four reporting ADHD, one autism), yielding a final sample of 78 participants.
text.formatted: Per preregistered criteria (18-35 years old, right-handed, fluent English speakers with normal or corrected vision and no cognitive, linguistic, or neurological conditions), nine were excluded (two for < 75% accuracy, two left-handed, four reporting ADHD, one autism), yielding a final sample of 78 participants.

text.text: All provided written informed consent and were compensated with $40 CAD or course credit.
All procedures were approved by the University of Toronto Research Ethics Board.

Forty-eight unique syllables were generated by pairing 16 consonants with one of four vowels (a, i, o, u), such that each consonant appeared once per list and each vowel appeared four times, yielding three balanced lists of 16 syllables.
text.formatted: Forty-eight unique syllables were generated by pairing 16 consonants with one of four vowels <ref type="bibr">(a, i, o, u)</ref>, such that each consonant appeared once per list and each vowel appeared four times, yielding three balanced lists of 16 syllables.

text.text: Lists were assigned to experimental conditions and counterbalanced across participants.

For visual presentation, each syllable was rendered as a 500 × 150 px image in Courier New font (in black, red, and blue) on a light gray background using a custom R script, ensuring uniform appearance across conditions.
Participants completed three conditions (Control, Frequency, and TP) in a counterbalanced within-subjects design.
In each condition, they first performed a Sustained Attention Task while viewing a continuous syllable stream.
The stream contained no regularities in the Control condition but encoded structured patterns in the Frequency and TP conditions.
After exposure to each of the two structured conditions, participants completed a Familiarity Judgment task followed by a Syllable Sorting task (task order fixed).
Participants were informed that the stream "may or may not contain a rule," and no information about the presence or nature of a pattern was provided before the Syllable Sorting task.
Before each new condition, they were told that any possible pattern would differ from earlier ones.
In each condition, participants were exposed to four syllable streams (i.e., blocks), interrupted by self-paced breaks.

Each block lasted 4 minutes and consisted of the continuous presentation of 960 syllables at a steady rate of 4 Hz (four syllables per second), resulting in a total of 16 minutes of exposure per condition.

Visual presentation was achieved through sinusoidal contrast modulation: syllables gradually increased in contrast against a light gray background, reaching maximum contrast (125 ms) and then decreasing back to baseline (250 ms, Fig. 1a).
text.formatted: Visual presentation was achieved through sinusoidal contrast modulation: syllables gradually increased in contrast against a light gray background, reaching maximum contrast (125 ms) and then decreasing back to baseline (250 ms, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">1a</ref>).

text.text: In the Control condition, syllables were displayed in pseudo-random order (avoiding close repetitions of the same syllable), and each one appeared exactly 60 times (960/16).
Crucially, this condition lacked any internal periodicity, apart from the fixed 4 Hz presentation rate of the syllables.
In the Frequency condition, the 16 syllables inside each list were arbitrarily divided into two equally sized groups: frequent (F) and infrequent (I).
These groups were uniquely generated for each participant.

A statistical regularity was introduced by manipulating the syllables' distribution within a stream: one syllable from the infrequent group was interleaved every three frequent syllables (e.g., F-F-F-I-F-F-F-I).

This manipulation created a frequency imbalance: in the absence of any other difference between both groups, and because each group contained an equal number of syllables, each frequent syllable was presented three times more often (90 times) than each syllable assigned to the infrequent group (30 times).
Lastly, in the TP condition, the 16 syllables were arbitrarily grouped into four sets of four-syllable-units (e.g., za-si-ro-bu, pa-ku-vi-fu).

These units were uniquely generated for each participant and presented sequentially in a pseudo-random order (i.e., no unit could repeat itself; all units were shown exactly 60 times) during a presentation block.
Within each unit, the TP between adjacent syllables (e.g., za-si) was 1.0, while the TP between syllables across unit boundaries (e.g., bu-pa) was 0.33.
In both structured conditions (Frequency, TP), statistical regularities occurred at a frequency of 1 Hz (i.e., every 4 syllables).

Thus, the main logic behind our manipulation is that, if participants were sensitive to the statistical structure of the streams, neural synchronization to the periodic statistical structure should emerge at 1 Hz in the structured streams, reflecting perceptual detection of statistical patterns, and not in the Control condition.
To measure fluctuations in sustained attention, participants performed a categorization task during exposure to the syllable streams (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: To measure fluctuations in sustained attention, participants performed a categorization task during exposure to the syllable streams (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">1b</ref>).

text.text: In each stream, 128 of the 960 syllables were colored instead of being black (i.e., in each block, 113 items appeared in red, and 15 appeared in blue), and participants were instructed to press one key (Z) when a red syllable appeared and another key (M) when a blue syllable appeared.
Importantly, any given syllable could appear in black, red, or blue within the same presentation block, as colors were not associated with any syllable.

Colored syllables (i.e., trials) were pseudo-randomly distributed throughout each stream, allowing participants adequate time to respond (i.e., at least one second) and ensuring no secondary statistical structure was created.

After exposure to each structured condition (Frequency, TP), participants completed a Familiarity Judgment Task, where they rated four-syllable strings (displayed simultaneously as a single unit; e.g., za-si-ro-bu) on a 4-point Likert scale based on whether they followed the same presentation order seen during the exposure phase.
Participants were not informed of the rule but were encouraged to make their best judgment.
Strings were categorized as correct, partially wrong, or completely wrong, with different constructions for each condition.

In the Frequency condition, correct strings followed the syllable frequency distribution from the exposure phase (F-F-F-I), partially wrong strings equated the frequency of the two groups (F-F-I-I), and completely wrong strings inverted the frequency pattern (F-I-I-I).
In the TP condition, correct strings were the same words presented during exposure (e.g., za-si-ro-bu).
Partially wrong strings concatenated syllables from two different words while preserving withinword transitional probabilities (e.g., ro-bu-pa-ku).
Completely wrong strings violated all transitional probabilities, with their relative position within the word preserved (e.g., za-ku-ni-ha).
Participants evaluated each string type (4 correct, 4 partially wrong, and 4 completely wrong) three times, in a blocked order with no time limit.

Following the Familiarity Judgment Task for the structured conditions, participants were informed about the statistical rule used to arrange the syllables in the exposure stream and were asked to perform a Syllable Sorting Task.
This task tested their acquired knowledge of the previously presented statistical structure by asking them to consciously retrieve the learned pattern from memory.
