Their task was to sort them into two boxes, labeled frequent and infrequent.
No information was provided regarding the number of syllables in each group, forcing participants to rely only on their knowledge of the frequency distribution.
In the TP condition, participants reconstructed the four units by dragging each syllable into one of four boxes and placing it in the correct serial position (1-4).
For both tasks, participants were given unlimited time but were required to sort every syllable before moving forward with the experiment.
Participants were individually tested in a dimly lit room and positioned in front of a ZOWIE XL LCD Windows monitor with a screen resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels, and a 60 Hz refresh rate.
Stimuli were presented using PsychToolbox-3 (Brainard, 1997), and were displayed at the center of the screen.
text.formatted: Stimuli were presented using PsychToolbox-3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brainard, 1997)</ref>, and were displayed at the center of the screen.

text.text: The keyboard and mouse were positioned in front of the participants.
Instructions for each task were provided both in writing and orally by the experimenter to ensure that participants fully understood the procedures.
Electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded with BioSemi ActiveTwo system (Biosemi, Amsterdam, Netherlands) at a sampling rate of 1024 Hz.
Sixty-four active electrodes were positioned on the scalp following the radial-ABC system using an elastic cap, while electrode offsets were maintained within ±20 mV.
Data were acquired unreferenced (BioSemi CMS/DRL).
Preprocessing was performed in MAT-LAB (The MathWorks Inc., 2024) through a combination of custom scripts and the EEGLAB toolbox (Delorme & Makeig, 2004).
text.formatted: Preprocessing was performed in MAT-LAB (The MathWorks Inc., 2024) through a combination of custom scripts and the EEGLAB toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Delorme & Makeig, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Data were first filtered with a 0.1-100 Hz band-pass filter.
We removed breaks between blocks to keep only the signal of interest, and we identified and removed channels exhibiting artifacts by visually inspecting the raw signal waveforms and power spectra.
Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was applied to remove ocular artifacts (blinks and saccades).
Rejected channels were reconstructed using spherical interpolation.
The continuous EEG was then segmented into 240-second epochs and re-referenced offline to the common average.
This procedure produced one dataset per participant, block (1-4), and condition (Control, Frequency, TP), with each block lasting 240 seconds.
Each dataset underwent a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), from which normalized amplitude spectra were derived for each channel.
Normalization involved taking the absolute value of the FFT and dividing it by the number of data points.
To reduce noise fluctuations across the frequency spectrum, thus mitigating the influence of boundary effects and outliers, a local baseline correction (BC) was applied.
Baseline at each frequency bin was computed as the mean of 80 neighboring bins (40 per side), excluding the three bins immediately adjacent to the target to avoid spectral leakage.
To ensure a robust estimate of the local noise floor, we further excluded the local minimum and maximum values within this window before averaging.
This mean was then subtracted from the observed amplitude.
The bin selection follows the same methodology established in previous studies (De Rosa et al., 2022), adjusted for the finer frequency resolution of this experiment (1/240 = 0.0042 Hz).
text.formatted: The bin selection follows the same methodology established in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(De Rosa et al., 2022)</ref>, adjusted for the finer frequency resolution of this experiment (1/240 = 0.0042 Hz).

text.text: Responses at our target frequencies were quantified as the combined BC amplitudes respectively at the syllable (4 Hz) and structure (1 Hz) stimulation frequencies, along with their first two harmonics (syllable: 8 Hz and 12 Hz; structure: 2 Hz and 3 Hz).
We investigated the EEG response to our syllable (4 Hz) and structure (1 Hz) frequencies.
First, the response to syllable stimulation frequency (4 Hz) was analyzed within the occipito-parietal region (Norcia et al., 2015) comprising 4 electrodes surrounding and including Oz.
text.formatted: First, the response to syllable stimulation frequency (4 Hz) was analyzed within the occipito-parietal region <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Norcia et al., 2015)</ref> comprising 4 electrodes surrounding and including Oz.

text.text: Then, for all three conditions we examined the EEG response to the pattern stimulation frequency (1 Hz) within two predefined regions of interest (ROIs).
These ROIs were selected based on prior research utilizing visual linguistic stimuli (De Rosa et al., 2022) and adapted for the lower number of overall electrodes.
text.formatted: These ROIs were selected based on prior research utilizing visual linguistic stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(De Rosa et al., 2022)</ref> and adapted for the lower number of overall electrodes.

text.text: The primary areas of interest for pattern responses included a cluster of six sites in both the left (focal point PO7) and right hemispheres (focal point PO8) and within the occipito-temporal region.

To evaluate whether neural entrainment was above the noise level within each condition, responses were first averaged across channels within each ROI for each participant, yielding four block-wise values, which were then averaged and subjected to one-sample t-tests, in keeping with previous work (De Rosa et al., 2022).
text.formatted: To evaluate whether neural entrainment was above the noise level within each condition, responses were first averaged across channels within each ROI for each participant, yielding four block-wise values, which were then averaged and subjected to one-sample t-tests, in keeping with previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(De Rosa et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For the structure-rate frequency (1 Hz), differences between conditions were assessed using a linear mixed-effects model in R (R Core Team, 2024), with the Control condition set as the reference level.

The model included condition (Control, Frequency, TP), ROI (left ROIs, right ROIs), and their interaction as fixed effects, as well as random intercepts for participants to account for within-subject variability.
The significance of effects was evaluated using Type II Wald χ 2 tests via the Anova function from the car package (Fox & Weisberg, 2019).
text.formatted: The significance of effects was evaluated using Type II Wald χ 2 tests via the Anova function from the car package <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Fox & Weisberg, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Planned pairwise comparisons were conducted using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026), with p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm correction.
text.formatted: Planned pairwise comparisons were conducted using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026)</ref>, with p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm correction.

text.text: To measure individual differences in sustained attention, we computed lapse rates as the proportion of trials in which participants were in a poor attentional state (i.e., out-of-zone), following previous work (Debettencourt et al., 2018; Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023; Esterman et al., 2013; Fortenbaugh et al., 2018).
text.formatted: To measure individual differences in sustained attention, we computed lapse rates as the proportion of trials in which participants were in a poor attentional state (i.e., out-of-zone), following previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Debettencourt et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Decker, Duncan, & Finn, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Esterman et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fortenbaugh et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We began by filtering the raw RT data obtained from our Sustained Attention Task, excluding trials with RTs shorter than 250 ms and longer than 1500 ms.
We then detrended RTs separately within each participant and block.
Specifically, for each participant × condition order × block order combination, we fit a linear model predicting RT from trial number within that block and extracted the residuals.

These residuals were then re-centered by adding each participant's overall mean RT, thereby removing within-block linear drift (e.g., practice or fatigue effects) while preserving individual differences in overall response speed.
Missing RTs were accounted for using moving-average interpolation based on the two preceding and two following trials.
Finally, for each trial, we computed the absolute deviation of the interpolated, residualized RT from the mean interpolated residualized RT within each participant, block and condition.
This triallevel deviance indexed attentional fluctuations.
A five-trial Gaussian-weighted moving average smoothed the data.
To establish a group-level threshold for attentional lapses, we first computed the median of this smoothed deviance for each participant and then averaged these medians across participants.
Trials above this threshold were labeled as out-of-zone, while the trials below the threshold were classified as in-zone.
Participants' lapse rates were operationalized as the proportion of out-of-zone trials out of the total number of trials (i.e., higher values reflected more time spent in a poor attentional state).
These values were then used for correlating lapses with neural entrainment across participants.
To validate the lapse index, we performed a linear mixed-effects model at the participant-by-condition level, treating participant as a random intercept.
A Type II Wald χ 2 test revealed that overall lapse rates significantly predicted categorization accuracy, χ 2 (1) = 9.10, p = .003.
In line with our predictions, higher lapse rates were associated with lower accuracy (b = -0.05, SE = 0.02, t = -3.02, p = .003).
We analyzed trial-level sustained-attention performance using generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) implemented in R (R Core Team, 2024) with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: We analyzed trial-level sustained-attention performance using generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) implemented in R (R Core Team, 2024) with the lme4 package <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The dependent variable (zone) indicated whether each trial was categorized as in-zone or out-of-zone.
The fixed-effects structure included condition, condition order, and block order, with a random intercept for participant.
The factor condition (Control, Frequency, and TP) was coded with Control as the reference level.
Significance of fixed effects was evaluated using Type II Wald χ 2 test via the Anova function from the car package (Fox & Weisberg, 2019).
text.formatted: Significance of fixed effects was evaluated using Type II Wald χ 2 test via the Anova function from the car package <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Fox & Weisberg, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Planned contrasts were performed using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026) to compare the Control condition against the Frequency and TP conditions, as well as comparing Frequency and TP conditions against each other.
text.formatted: Planned contrasts were performed using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026)</ref> to compare the Control condition against the Frequency and TP conditions, as well as comparing Frequency and TP conditions against each other.

text.text: Resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm correction.
Predicted probabilities and 95% confidence intervals were extracted from the model to generate effects plots using ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016).
text.formatted: Predicted probabilities and 95% confidence intervals were extracted from the model to generate effects plots using ggplot2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Wickham, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To assess the relationship between sustained attention and neural entrainment, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) predicting structure-rate entrainment (1 Hz) from lapse rate, condition, and their interaction, with a random intercept for participant.
Structure-rate entrainment was quantified by averaging the BC sum of the target frequency (1 Hz) and its two higher harmonics (2 and 3 Hz) across the four exposure blocks within each condition.

Planned contrasts of the interaction slopes were then performed using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026) to compare the Control condition with the Frequency and TP conditions, with p-values adjusted using the Holm correction.
text.formatted: Planned contrasts of the interaction slopes were then performed using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026)</ref> to compare the Control condition with the Frequency and TP conditions, with p-values adjusted using the Holm correction.

text.text: To test whether within-subject, trial-by-trial fluctuations in sustained attention were accompanied by corresponding changes in neural entrainment, we conducted a complementary analysis using Inter-Trial-Coherence (ITC), preregistered as exploratory, within the Frequency and TP conditions.

This analysis was considered exploratory because attentional states were not experimentally imposed and because it required reconstructing in-zone and out-of-zone periods into continuous stretches containing complete pattern cycles.
We used ITC rather than spectral power because the zeropadding required to preserve complete structure cycles maintains phase alignment but can alter amplitude estimates.

Starting from the interpolated and re-referenced data, EEG data were low-pass filtered at 30 Hz, to align with previous work (Batterink & Paller, 2017), and segmented into continuous stretches that remained entirely within the same attentional state, as determined from the behavioral lapse classification procedure.
text.formatted: Starting from the interpolated and re-referenced data, EEG data were low-pass filtered at 30 Hz, to align with previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Batterink & Paller, 2017)</ref>, and segmented into continuous stretches that remained entirely within the same attentional state, as determined from the behavioral lapse classification procedure.

text.text: Stretches spanning different attentional states were excluded to avoid ambiguity in state assignment.
Within each stretch, data were aligned to the underlying four-syllable structure using syllable boundaries.
Because some stretches began or ended mid-word, incomplete initial or final portions were zero-padded to preserve phase alignment.
The resulting data were then split into in-zone and out-of-zone subsets, from which 6s epochs were extracted, corresponding to 24 syllables and six complete structure cycles.

We verified that the in-zone and out-of-zone subsets were comparable in total duration and number of extracted epochs, despite minor differences in the number of contributing stretches and the proportion of zero-padding (see Supplementary Table 3 for details).
text.formatted: We verified that the in-zone and out-of-zone subsets were comparable in total duration and number of extracted epochs, despite minor differences in the number of contributing stretches and the proportion of zero-padding (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> for details).

text.text: To compute ITC, the Fast Fourier transform (FFT) was first applied to each reconstructed in-zone and out-of-zone 6-s epoch.

ITC was computed by extracting the complex Fourier coefficients for each epoch, normalizing each coefficient by its magnitude to obtain unit phase vectors, and then averaging the resulting phase vectors across epochs within each attentional state.
To express observed ITC relative to a null distribution, we generated subject-and zone-specific surrogate distributions using phase-rotation time shifts.

In each of 250 iterations, epochs were circularly shifted in time within ±700 ms via frequency-domain phase rotation, which preserves spectral properties while disrupting temporal alignment across epochs.

Because surrogate distributions were computed separately for each participant and attentional state using the corresponding number of epochs, resulting z-scored ITC estimates were less susceptible to residual differences in data quantity across subsets.

ITC was recomputed and observed ITC values were converted to z-scores using the corresponding surrogate mean and standard deviation. z-ITC values were averaged across predefined ROIs and summed across the 1-Hz structure frequency and its higher harmonics (2 Hz and 3 Hz).
We then fit a linear mixed-effects model predicting z-ITC from condition, attentional zone, and their interaction, with random intercepts for participants.
We analyzed participants' familiarity ratings using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs), separately for the Frequency and TP conditions.

For each condition, familiarity ratings were modeled as a function of string type (correct, partially wrong, completely wrong) and repetition number (1-3) as fixed effects, with a random intercept for participant.
Post-hoc pairwise comparisons between string types were conducted using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026) with pairwise contrasts to examine differences in familiarity ratings.
text.formatted: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons between string types were conducted using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026)</ref> with pairwise contrasts to examine differences in familiarity ratings.

text.text: In the Frequency condition, accuracy was calculated as the mean proportion of syllables correctly classified as frequent or infrequent.
Accuracy scores were averaged across participants, and a one-sample t-test was conducted to compare performance against the 50% chance level.
In the TP condition, accuracy reflects the proportion of adjacent within-unit transitions preserved in the correct relative order.

For each four-syllable unit, transitions between consecutive syllables (e.g., 1-2, 2-3, and 3-4) were scored as correct only when the syllables were placed in the same box and in adjacent positions in the correct order.
Transition scores were averaged across units to obtain a mean TP accuracy score for each participant.

Due to the lack of an analytical chance level, chance performance was estimated via 1000 simulations of random syllable arrangements that respected the constraints of the sorting task (i.e., each of the 16 syllables was randomly assigned to one of the 16 available slots, with exactly four syllables per box), yielding a chance benchmark of 5.01%.
Participants' mean TP accuracy was compared against this simulated chance level using a one-sample t-test.
Neural entrainment at the syllable rate reflected low-level synchronization to the periodic input and was present in all conditions (all ps < .001; see Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics).
text.formatted: Neural entrainment at the syllable rate reflected low-level synchronization to the periodic input and was present in all conditions (all ps < .001; see Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for full statistics).

text.text: By contrast, neural entrainment at the structure rate reflected sensitivity to the statistical structure embedded in the syllable sequences (Fig. 2a).
text.formatted: By contrast, neural entrainment at the structure rate reflected sensitivity to the statistical structure embedded in the syllable sequences (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref>).

text.text: As expected, the Control condition showed no evidence of entrainment at this frequency (both ps > .05), whereas both structured conditions (Frequency and TP) showed reliable entrainment (all ps < .001; see Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1).
text.formatted: As expected, the Control condition showed no evidence of entrainment at this frequency (both ps > .05), whereas both structured conditions (Frequency and TP) showed reliable entrainment (all ps < .001; see Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> and Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We directly tested whether within-subject fluctuations in sustained attention were accompanied by corresponding changes in neural entrainment.

A Type II Wald χ 2 test on z-ITC revealed significant main effects of attentional zone, χ 2 (1) = 9.25, p = .002, and condition, χ 2 (1) = 42.39, p < .001, indicating greater neural entrainment during in-zone than out-of-zone periods (Fig. 2d) and higher entrainment in the TP than in the Frequency condition.

text.text: The interaction between zone (in-vs. out-zone) and condition was not significant, χ 2 (1) = 2.13, p = .144.

These findings extend the between-participant results by showing that not only do individuals with fewer attentional lapses exhibit higher overall neural entrainment, but trial-by-trial fluctuations in attention within a given individual also covary with corresponding changes in neural tracking.
To assess learning, we used two complementary measures: familiarity ratings and a syllable sorting task.
Considering the Frequency condition first, familiarity ratings (Fig. 3a) showed only a marginal effect of string type (correct, partially wrong, completely wrong), χ 2 (2) = 5.10, p = .078.

However, sorting accuracy (M = 0.55, SD = 0.15; Fig. 3b) was significantly above chance (0.50), t = 2.59, p = .011, d = 0.29, 95% CI [0.51, 0.58], indicating reliable discrimination of frequency-based structure beyond initial exposure on one of two measures.

text.text: The ability to track regularities in the environment is a fundamental feature of human cognition, shaping representations and processing across domains including language (Batterink & Paller, 2017 ), vision (De Rosa et al., 2022), and music (Van Hedger et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The ability to track regularities in the environment is a fundamental feature of human cognition, shaping representations and processing across domains including language <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Batterink & Paller, 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr">), vision (De Rosa et al., 2022)</ref>, and music <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Van Hedger et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In this work, we investigated its internal dynamics by testing whether the brain's sensitivity to structure varies alongside naturally occurring fluctuations in one's attentional state.
We found that lapses in attention are associated with concurrent reductions in neural entrainment to the regularities.

This was observed both between individuals-that is, people with more lapses tend to show reduced entrainment overall-and within individuals-manifested as enhanced entrainment during periods of heightened attentional focus.
These findings speak directly to a central question in the field: whether attention matters for statistical learning.
It matters greatly.

Indeed, our within-subject analysis reveals that neural entrainment is reduced when individuals are in a worse attentional state, providing strong evidence that attention dynamically interacts with the online processing of statistical regularities.
This is very much in line with other work showing that one's attentional state shapes learning outcomes more generally (Cowan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is very much in line with other work showing that one's attentional state shapes learning outcomes more generally <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cowan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings also suggest that the relationship between statistical learning and attention may be reciprocal; while heightened attentional focus is accompanied by enhanced entrainment, the presence of statistical regularities concurrently helps capture and stabilize focus, consistent with evidence that attention is spontaneously biased toward structure (Zhao et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The present findings also suggest that the relationship between statistical learning and attention may be reciprocal; while heightened attentional focus is accompanied by enhanced entrainment, the presence of statistical regularities concurrently helps capture and stabilize focus, consistent with evidence that attention is spontaneously biased toward structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Zhao et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is specifically supported by our finding that attentional engagement was significantly higher during the presentation of structured versus random visual streams.

Within this framework, neural entrainment does not merely reflect a passive downstream effect of attention; instead, it may index a dynamic interplay in which sensitivity to structure and attentional state covary over time.
This aligns with previous research showing that attention itself is not static, but appears to fluctuate in response to the richness, predictability, or entropy of the input (Forest et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This aligns with previous research showing that attention itself is not static, but appears to fluctuate in response to the richness, predictability, or entropy of the input <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Forest et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: If attentional engagement depends on the predictability of the input, it follows that different types of statistical structures may influence attentional states and neural entrainment in distinct ways.

Indeed, this work also shows that both attentional states and neural entrainment varied based on the type of structure that was being presented: they were greater for TP-based than frequency-based regularities.

This is noteworthy since the statistical learning literature has focused for years on the former (Frost et al., 2019), building on the original paradigm introduced by Saffran and colleagues (Saffran et al., 1996).
text.formatted: This is noteworthy since the statistical learning literature has focused for years on the former <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Frost et al., 2019)</ref>, building on the original paradigm introduced by Saffran and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Saffran et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: However, our perceptual input is very rich and includes regularities of many different sorts.
Recently, one of these regularities, that is, item frequency, has attracted some attention (De Rosa et al., 2022; Growns et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Recently, one of these regularities, that is, item frequency, has attracted some attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(De Rosa et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Growns et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Zhou et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This considerably extends the remit of statistical learning and its potential role in other cognitive functions; for example, word frequency was suggested to be at the basis of the distinction between grammatical classes, one of the fundamental ingredients of proficient language use (Mintz, 2003; Reeder et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This considerably extends the remit of statistical learning and its potential role in other cognitive functions; for example, word frequency was suggested to be at the basis of the distinction between grammatical classes, one of the fundamental ingredients of proficient language use <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mintz, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Reeder et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, TP-based and frequency-based regularities also differ in the level at which prediction operates.
In our Frequency condition, participants could anticipate the likely occurrence of a syllable category (frequent vs. infrequent) but had no basis for predicting which specific item would appear next.
By contrast, in our TP condition, each element strongly constrained the identity of the following one, supporting fine-grained, item-level predictions.

Overall, frequency-based and TP-based statistics may support different computational goals within statistical learning, yielding broad sensitivity to environmental regularities on the one hand, and precise internal models of sequential structure on the other.
Crucially, however, the impact of attentional lapses on neural entrainment to structured input was comparable across structured conditions and in both our betweenand within-participants analyses.

This convergence suggests that while the brain may prioritize and encode these structures via different predictive levels, the link between sustained attention and neural tracking may reflect a constraint that operates independently of the type of statistical structure.

These results point to a robust coupling between attentional states and the extraction of statistical regularities and highlight the need for future work to determine the principles that govern which types of statistical structures are most readily encoded and tracked by the brain.

As a final note, we highlight the contrast between the very strong entrainment that we observed here and the scattered signs of behavioral learning, which were quite weak and only emerged in some tasks and contrasts.

This result echoes prior differences that have been shown between neural entrainment and behavior (Benjamin et al., 2025; Herrera-Chaves et al., 2026; Moser et al., 2021), and suggests that this type of statistical learning may produce memory representations that are relatively fleeting or not easily accessible, at least under typical exposure conditions.
text.formatted: This result echoes prior differences that have been shown between neural entrainment and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Benjamin et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Herrera-Chaves et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Moser et al., 2021)</ref>, and suggests that this type of statistical learning may produce memory representations that are relatively fleeting or not easily accessible, at least under typical exposure conditions.

text.text: This resonates with an articulated view of the neural and cognitive mechanisms that lie behind statistical learning (Batterink & Paller, 2017; Thiessen et al., 2013) and invites further research to understand how transient neural tracking transitions into accessible behavioral knowledge.
text.formatted: This resonates with an articulated view of the neural and cognitive mechanisms that lie behind statistical learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Thiessen et al., 2013)</ref> and invites further research to understand how transient neural tracking transitions into accessible behavioral knowledge.

text.text: Together, these findings show that the human brain is highly sensitive to statistical structure, capable of detecting different types of regularities even under rapid and continuous input.

At the same time, this sensitivity appears to be tempered by one's attentional state, contrary to more simplistic views of statistical learning as an encapsulated, attention-independent mechanism that automatically translates regularities into new memory representations (Batterink & Paller, 2019; Duncan & Theeuwes, 2020): neural tracking is shaped by the type of regularity presented and covaries with fluctuations in attentional engagement.
text.formatted: At the same time, this sensitivity appears to be tempered by one's attentional state, contrary to more simplistic views of statistical learning as an encapsulated, attention-independent mechanism that automatically translates regularities into new memory representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Batterink & Paller, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Duncan & Theeuwes, 2020)</ref>: neural tracking is shaped by the type of regularity presented and covaries with fluctuations in attentional engagement.

text.text: This early index of statistical learning, therefore, appears to be the result of a dynamic interplay between perceptual and attentional mechanisms.

1 Relationship between online (structure-rate neural entrainment) and offline (familiarity scores) measures of statistical learning

To assess the relationship between structure-rate neural entrainment (1 Hz) and offline behavioral learning, as assessed via the familiarity judgment task, we fit linear models predicting two different familiarity scores from neural entrainment amplitude, condition (Frequency vs.
TP), and their interaction.
Specifically, we first focused on the traditionally used familiarity score, calculated as the mean of correct (C) minus completely wrong (CW) syllable strings.
We then looked at a different learning score that reflects participants' discrimination accuracy between correct and partially wrong (PW) syllable strings.
Significance of effects was evaluated using Type II F -tests implemented via the Anova function from the car package.

For the contrast between correct and completely wrong items, the linear model revealed no main effect of structure-rate neural entrainment, F (1, 152) = 1.34, p = .249, and no main effect of condition, F (1, 152) = 0.006, p = .940.
The interaction between structure-rate neural entrainment and condition was significant, F (1, 152) = 4.72, p = .031.

Follow-up Pearson correlations indicated that higher neural entrainment at 1 Hz was associated with higher familiarity scores in the Frequency condition (r = 0.24, p = .036), but not in the TP condition (r = -0.12, p = .294).

Considering the contrast between correct and partially wrong strings, the model revealed a significant effect of structure-rate neural entrainment, F (1, 152) = 6.57, p = .011, no main effect of condition, F (1, 152) = 0.12, p = .725, and no significant interaction between neural entrainment and condition, F (1, 152) = 0.001, p = .895.

We investigated whether participants were able to group syllables solely on the basis of their absolute position within a sequence.
For each participant, we computed Position Accuracy as the proportion of syllables correctly placed in their exact target position, irrespective of correct syllable grouping.
Because each syllable had four possible position slots, chance performance was 25%.
To test whether participants tracked positional information, we conducted a one-sample ttest comparing mean observed position accuracy against the 25% chance baseline.
Participants correctly placed syllables in their target position 31.33% of the time (SD = 14.30%), performing significantly above chance, t(77) = 3.91, p < .001, d = 0.44.
text.formatted: Participants correctly placed syllables in their target position 31.33% of the time (SD = 14.30%), performing significantly above chance, t(77) = 3.91, p < .001, d = 0.44.

text.text: This indicates that participants successfully sorted syllables according to their absolute ordinal position.
We investigated whether position of colored syllables (1-4) within a sequence influenced participants' attentional states.
To test this, we fit a generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) with a binomial distribution, predicting Zone (in-zone vs. out-of-zone).
The model included Condition (Control, Frequency, TP), Syllable Position (treated as a 4-level categorical factor: 1, 2, 3, 4), and their interaction as fixed effects.
Participant was included as a random intercept to account for repeated measures.
A Type II Wald χ 2 test revealed, as expected, a significant main effect of Condition, χ 2 (2) = 77.86, p < .001.
text.formatted: A Type II Wald χ 2 test revealed, as expected, a significant main effect of Condition, χ 2 (2) = 77.86, p < .001.

text.text: Crucially, we observed no significant main effect of Syllable Position, χ 2 (3) = 1.81, p = .612, nor was there a significant interaction between Condition and Syllable Position, χ 2 (6) = 6.73, p = .346.
These results indicate that participants' attentional state was not systematically influenced by the colored syllable's ordinal position, nor did the effect of position vary by condition.

text.text: Fig 3 Familiarity ratings by string type (a) and sorting accuracy (b) in the Frequency (left) and TP (right) conditions.
Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals, and asterisks denote statistically significant contrasts.
In panel b (right), the shaded green band represents the 95% simulation-based chance interval (5.01%) used as a reference for TP sorting accuracy.
Figure 1: Frequency spectra and scalp distributions of baseline-corrected (BC) EEG amplitude.
(A) EEG amplitude spectra: BC amplitude spectra are shown for the Control (orange), Frequency (blue), and TP (green) conditions, averaged across the left and right ROIs.
Dashed vertical lines mark the structure frequency and its first two harmonics (1, 2, and 3 Hz).

For visualization purposes, a white separator with 80% opacity was inserted between the overlapping Frequency and TP peaks at the harmonic frequencies to facilitate visual discrimination; the separator does not alter the underlying amplitudes or their relative heights.
(B) Scalp topographies: Topographies depict the summed baseline-corrected amplitude across 1, 2, and 3 Hz.

Maps correspond to the Control, Frequency, and TP conditions (left to right, indicated by colored panel borders), displayed using identical color limits ranging from white (0 µV) to the maximum condition-specific color intensity (0.15 µV).
Figure 2: Relationship between structure-rate neural entrainment (1 Hz) and familiarity scores (C-CW) separately for Frequency (left) and TP (right) conditions.
Points represent individual participants.
Reported statistics are Pearson correlation coefficients.
Solid lines show leastsquares fits with shaded 95% confidence intervals.
Figure 4: Relationship between lapse rates and familiarity scores (C-CW) separately for Frequency (left) and TP (right) conditions.
Points represent individual participants.
Reported statistics are Pearson correlation coefficients.
Solid lines show least-squares fits with shaded 95% confidence intervals.

This study is closely based on De Rosa et al. (2022), so we planned from the beginning to follow the same pre-processing pipeline.
We judge this issue to have no impact on the Results; it was essentially an oversight on our part during the write-up of the pre-registration document.
